# IUPAC drawing rules

Interpret "preferred", "acceptable", and "not acceptable" at their stated strength: preferences define defaults and trigger warnings, not failures.
These recommendations apply to individual structures; reaction schemes may require different orientations.
Clarity and legibility take priority; apply the stated exceptions when necessary.

Default angles have a ±10° tolerance; deviations trigger warnings unless a depiction is explicitly forbidden.

The scripts enforce all other IUPAC rules automatically.

## Text, lines, color, size

- Do not create new abbreviations whose meaning depends on text formatting; both roman and italic P remain acceptable in biochemical diagrams.
- Use clear, distinct colors for emphasis (typically red); avoid dark blue or dark gray on a predominantly black structure.
- Strongly avoid pairing red and green as contrasting colors in the same diagram.
- Scale diagrams and their labels uniformly in both dimensions; do not shrink labels to an illegible size.
- To fit a structure on a page, rotate part of it around a single bond (preferably attached to a ring, or else near mid-chain), keep one part in its standard orientation, or abbreviate parts.

## Bonds

- Do not use a bare terminal bond to indicate an unspecified or variable attachment.
- Use bent bonds only for carbohydrate linkages (smooth curves, never sharp corners; straight, slightly angled bonds are preferred for Haworth glycosidic linkages) and cyclic-peptide closures (sharp corners).
- Do not indicate coordination merely by placing unconnected fragments in proximity.
- At a coordinated atom of specified configuration, draw wedged or hashed bonds just as at any other stereocenter.
- Use a wedged or hashed bond to a delocalized system only to indicate the distant atom's configuration; prefer plain bonds if other substituents can carry the stereobonds.
- Represent multi-center bonding with ordinary two-atom bonds rather than curves.

## Atom labels

- Show an unpaired electron or charge explicitly rather than by omitting an H atom.
- Draw H atoms with explicit bonds only where needed or specifically chosen; fold other H atoms into atom labels by default.
- A carbon bonded to two heteroatoms by one single and one triple bond may be labeled or left unlabeled.
- Use a dot for carbon only between the double bonds of an allene, drawn large and clear of the bonds; placing a dot next to a non-carbon, or drawing two double bonds on opposite sides, is not acceptable.
- Preferably label the terminal carbons of a partial structure.
- A terminal carbon on a heteroatom may be labeled as CH3 or Me (never C), but do not mix both in the same diagram.
- Label terminal carbons attached to unlabeled carbons only where no overlap occurs.
- Avoid combining multiple isotopes of an element in one label; if unavoidable, list the natural-abundance symbol first, followed by isotopes in order of increasing mass, and use a consistent notation for D and T.
- Indicate partial isotopic labeling by placing square brackets around the element symbol only.
- Use Me, Et, Pr, iPr, Bu, iBu, s-Bu, t-Bu, Ac, Ph, Ms, Ts, and Cp freely, but only for the exact unsubstituted, uncharged, radical-free, natural-isotope group; clearly define all other abbreviations.
- Restrict Ac, Cm, Nb, Np, and Pr to organic contexts; do not create abbreviations that match an element symbol or redefine a common abbreviation; avoid Bz; use Cp only when coordinated to a metal.
- Use multi-attachment abbreviations with care: place the N-terminus on the left and the C-terminus on the right, and avoid two-line cyclic peptides.
- Use single-letter abbreviations only where the meaning is clear; single Latin letters next to atoms and bonds are not acceptable (use multi-letter abbreviations instead, except italic P in biochemical diagrams); phi for phenyl is acceptable.
- When clarity is critical and space allows, prefer fully expanded structures over contracted labels.
- Attach at most two bonds to a contracted label, both horizontal and at its first and last symbols, never to interior symbols.
- Write a contracted label to be read outward from its bond, satisfying normal valences; avoid attaching a bond on the right unless the label has four or fewer symbols, and avoid long labels bonded at their last symbol.
- Avoid contracted labels containing S, Se, Te, P, or other variable-valence elements, especially before chalcogens or halogens; use SO2, SeO2, and TeO2 only for sulfones, selenones, and tellurones; never put transition metals, Ga, In, Tl, noble gases, lanthanides, or actinides in a contracted label; draw them with explicit bonds instead.
- Interpret CH2 in a label as an in-chain link; draw a branching methylidene with explicit bonds or as (=CH2) in a label.
- Enclose branches in parentheses (beginning with an equals sign for a double-bonded branch, which may be omitted for a single O, S, Se, or Te atom); nesting is allowed, but avoid overly complex labels.
- Avoid explicit single bonds inside contracted labels.
- Use CHO, COO–, CO2–, COOH, CO2H, CN, NC, OCN, NCO, CNO, ONC, NO2, ONO, N2, N3, PO3H2, PO3 2–, SO3–, SO3H, and CO (and their chalcogen analogs) freely in contracted labels, with their implicit charges.
- Place single-attachment abbreviations and functional-group strings last in a label or parenthesized group; order components as H first, then element symbols alphabetically, abbreviations, and multi-symbol fragments.
- Do not write labels that show only element counts without implying connectivity.
- Use formulas (read left to right) only for simple molecules; prefer structural diagrams for organic molecules with more than one carbon.

## Orientation

- Place principal functional groups (acyclic heteroatoms) toward the right; draw esters with the parent acid portion toward the right.
- Place the principal ring system toward the bottom left, and spread substituents horizontally rather than vertically.
- Place a doubly bonded substituent on a horizontal chain above the chain, even if the zigzag direction changes.
- Reorient components to highlight relationships such as electron movement, even if this overrides their preferred isolated orientation.
- Draw isolated rings of nine or more atoms with reentrant (puckered) angles (120° preferred; otherwise 108°, 129°, or 135°); depict every double bond in its correct configuration, place as many substituents outside as possible, point unsubstituted heteroatoms inward, and keep triple bonds linear.
- Draw fused rings abutting at their shared bond, with each ring's atoms outside the other; preserve symmetry and maximize undistorted six-membered rings; a distorted five-membered ring may be drawn as a truncated hexagon, and large rings should be fused cis-like.
- Draw bridged systems as a simple or fused ring system with bridges: maximize undistorted six-membered rings, avoid exact overlap, keep every ring sharing a bond visible, and minimize substituents on bridges. Keep embedded rings in phanes regular. Arrange rings sharing two bonds to minimize distortion in both (with both shared bonds trans-like relative to the larger ring), and arrange rings sharing three bonds with the outer two trans-like and the central one cis-like.
- Select the principal ring system by priority: most fused rings, largest rings, highest unsaturation, most heteroatoms, or greatest chemical importance.
- Orient isolated 3-, 4-, 5-, 7-, and 8-membered rings with a horizontal bond at the top or bottom, and six-membered rings with a vertical bond on the left. Orient fused systems horizontally with a vertical or horizontal symmetry axis, placing extra rings toward the top and right, larger rings on the left, and heteroatoms toward the right (and slightly downward). Orient rings of nine or more atoms like the corresponding fused systems.
- Prefer established class-specific orientations (amino acids, carbohydrates, steroids, tetrapyrroles, carotenoids, natural products, and polymers).
- Position double bonds in isolated rings toward the left and then the top (subordinate to fused-ring orientation rules); draw either resonance form for alternating rings, keeping symmetric structures symmetric.

## Substituent positions

- Draw a single bond collinear with a double bond (for unknown cis/trans configuration) only when the double bond has a single substituent at each end and both single bonds are collinear with the double bond.
- Reserve four bonds at 45° to the horizontal and vertical axes for square-planar complexes.
- Use the 30°/105°/105°/120° angle pattern only to emphasize tetrahedral geometry (e.g., in phosphate-type groups), and only when the two substituents separated by 30° are graphically small; draw one of the remaining bonds strictly vertical or horizontal.
- A cis chain double bond may be drawn with 150° angles only to preserve chain linearity when it has no further substituents; using 120° at the double bond and 105° to the chain bonds is acceptable, not preferred.
- Draw a substituent on an external ring-fusion atom outside the ring system, bisecting the external angle (for substituents of more than three atoms, snap to a multiple of 30° if within 6°).
- When two adjacent fusion atoms are substituted, draw one substituent inside the ring system, oriented vertically or horizontally. A substituent adjacent to an unsubstituted fusion atom goes outside if all substituents can fit outside, or is drawn vertically or horizontally if another substituent is inside. Never place two substituents inside a ring of fewer than eight atoms, and place none inside at a fusion atom lacking a vertical or horizontal fusion bond. Place substituents on interior fusion atoms, as well as small substituents at steroid C-8 and C-9, inside the ring system.
- At a spiro atom, keep the two ring bisectors collinear and neither ring distorted.
- Draw three or more substituents on a ring atom at equal angles, or use the recommended non-tetrahedral configuration styles when configuration matters.
- For rings drawn in perspective, draw their substituents in the same perspective.
- Whenever possible, draw large rings so that substituted atoms point outward (convex) and no substituent sits at a reentrant vertex; only ring nitrogens in macrocycles intended for complexation may point inward.
- Resolve overlap in this order: move a small substituent to the other side of a large one; rotate around a chain bond (smallest change; never around a stereogenic double bond); swap neighboring groups; bend or stretch spiro junctions; adjust the perspective of a planar ring; lengthen a bond; adjust a substituent bond angle; or rotate a small substituent among its three positions.
- Do not alter the perspective of a planar ring that bears additional substituents.
- Lengthen the base–sugar bond in nucleosides and nucleotides as a stylistic convention.

## Charges, lone pairs, unpaired electrons

- Use delocalized representations to reflect actual electronic structure; assign a charge or unpaired electron to a specific atom when illustrating localized mechanisms.
- A charged carbon may be left unlabeled, though labeling it is preferred.
- Lewis structures are strongly discouraged outside teaching contexts.
- Place a radical dot on the atom of highest spin density, if possible.
- Draw delocalized charges and unpaired electrons as separate symbols centered in the delocalized system, or at the top-right corner.
- Omit partial charges unless emphasizing polarity; place δ+ and δ– near the atoms (with at least one of each in a neutral molecule), and format partial charges of specified numerical value like integral charges.
- Avoid mixing formal and partial charges; using partial charges to show a net formal charge delocalized by resonance is not acceptable.
- Write a polyatomic ion either as its formula in square brackets with a superscript charge after the closing bracket, or as a full structure inside large square brackets (for a single fragment, a top-right corner bracket may replace the left bracket, provided the charge cannot be misread as belonging to a structure on the left).
- Avoid other localized-charge depictions of polyatomic ions.

## Delocalization

- Draw a delocalization curve centered in the system, at least one bond width from each bond and at most twice the double-bond spacing; it need not be circular, convex, or closed.
- Draw delocalization curves solid and as wide as a single bond.
- Use curves only to depict delocalization, never for systems whose electrons are primarily localized.
- A curve represents only the delocalized electrons spanning its adjacent bonds; indicate any additional unsaturation with explicit bonds (e.g., replacing a single bond with a double bond).
- Prefer localized bonds for furan and pyrrole (curves are acceptable).
- Prefer curves for delocalized systems that cannot be represented by alternating single and double bonds.
- Do not place curves in two adjacent fused rings; place a curve only in the ring known to be delocalized.

## Salts

- Place a monoatomic ion beside its counterion or aligned as if bonded to it (the cation may be on the right); place larger components side by side, with the cation left of the anion when similar in size, or the larger component left of the smaller.
- Stack multiple small components vertically, up to the height of the tallest component.
- Prefer drawing identical fragments once with a leading stoichiometric number; drawing all copies explicitly is acceptable.
- For salts of unspecified form, bracket the largest ions on the left and the others on the right, about one bond length apart; write repeat counts as a leading number before a formula or a subscript after the closing bracket of a structure.
- Draw salts of neutral components (e.g., hydrochlorides) without brackets, placing the larger component on the left and the smaller on the right; a centered dot before a small formula is optional.
- Write a repeat count in regular type before its formula, separated by a space; separate a centered dot from the formula by a space, but not from the repeat count.
- Draw the neutral parent structure plus HCl when the protonation site is variable.

## Dative bonds and charge-separated forms

- Draw azides and diazo compounds with two double bonds, placing N– at the terminus and N+ adjacent to it; a single and a triple bond is acceptable.
- Draw phosphates, arsenates, sulfoxides, sulfones, sulfimides, and similar groups (including as anions) with ordinary single and double bonds and no extra charges (octet expansion is accepted); prefer the double-bonded form of chalcogen heterocycles over zwitterions.

## Variable attachment

- Draw variable (Markush) structures as a core with marked positions and substituent lists; place the list below or to the right of the parent structure, and always below within a reaction scheme.
- Mark positions with R and a superscript number or primes (never subscripts); X, Z, and G are also allowed; use distinct labels where substituents may differ, as sites vary independently.
- Connect each variable substituent by a single bond; use multiple bonds only when every listed item is monoatomic or symmetric; lists that change the bonding pattern are not acceptable.
- Enclose in-label lists in brackets and keep them short; prefer simple lists over prose text, and use tables for large sets.
- Indicate a substituent at a variable ring position with a bond extending into the ring center; bonds for independent substituents must not join.
- Use Alk, Alkyl, Ar, Aryl, E, EWG, M, Nu, and Q strictly for their defined classes; avoid accompanying text, which may only restrict a class, never redefine it; strongly avoid Ar where it could be read as argon; use R and X generically or with explanatory text.
- Write a homogeneous chain of variable length as bracketed CH2 with a subscript range; curved lines for variable ring size are acceptable.
- Use variable attachment positions only on a known ring at an H-bearing atom.
- Indicate a fragment's attachment point with an explicit, unambiguous bond; never imply it by a missing H or an altered bond length.

## Annotations

- Avoid asterisks (for stereocenters, isotopes, or excited states); if used, explain them in the text.
- Place bond annotations near the bond midpoint.

## Pseudobonds and coordination polyhedra

- Draw macromolecule backbone pseudobonds so they are clearly distinct from ordinary bonds.
- Draw connectors as curved bonds between the relevant atoms; a four-spoke wheel of 90° segments is acceptable, and sometimes preferred, for tetrapyrrole metal complexes.

## Linear drawing style

- Use the linear style (horizontal and vertical bonds only) solely for simple structures; it is not acceptable for general use.
- In this style, label every atom (including C and H), make bonds long enough to be clearly visible, place substituents above the chain, maintain a consistent style across a structure and group of structures, and draw rings explicitly, keeping bonds to the linear portion horizontal or vertical; align a bond on the right side of a label with its last character.

## Stereochemistry: plain bonds, wedges, hashes, wavy bonds

- A wavy bond at a carbohydrate anomeric carbon indicates a mixture of anomers; do not extend this usage to other compound classes.
- Draw mixtures of diastereomers as separate explicit structures, with explanatory text if needed.
- Drawing a stereocenter with three plain bonds and one wedge (pointing to the graphically smallest substituent) is preferred only in fused or bridged rings, or when one substituent is much larger than the others; elsewhere it is merely acceptable.
- Prefer the two-wedge style when two acyclic substituents are similar in size.
- Place the graphically larger of two non-identical horizontal substituents on the right.
- A 90° alternating wedge pattern is acceptable, not preferred; avoid alternating patterns at any other angles.
- Do not place the wedge of a three-bond stereocenter inside the smaller (<180°) angle between its two plain bonds, except at a bridgehead bond of a bridged ring system, where this placement is preferred.
- A three-bond center with one plain, one solid, and one hashed wedge separated by a gap of 180° or more is acceptable, not preferred.
- An explicit H atom at a stereocenter is always acceptable.
- At bridgeheads, wedge or hash the bridging bonds and draw the bridgehead substituent plain (or with the same wedge or hash type); do not wedge only the substituent. At other ring stereocenters, keep the ring bonds plain.
- At spiro stereocenters, draw one ring's bonds plain and the other's with one solid and one hashed wedge (placing the wedges on the smaller or more distorted ring); avoid wedges on bonds connecting two stereocenters.
- At an atom shared by both a regular fusion and a spiro union, place one solid and one hashed wedge on the two bonds not in the regular fusion and keep the two regular-fusion bonds plain.
- Do not depict tetrahedral configuration at reentrant ring atoms when any alternative exists (epoxide wedges at reentrant angles are not acceptable); if unavoidable, point substituents inward, and swap solid and hashed wedges if the atom is redrawn as convex.
- At a stereocenter with multiple bonds, place wedges on the single-bonded ligands; avoid wedged double bonds.
- Draw axial chirality in an even cumulene like a tetrahedral stereocenter, never with stereobonds at both ends and preferably showing all four substituents (an implicit H on an unlabeled carbon is acceptable); use three plain bonds and one wedge only adjacent to another stereocenter.
- Draw hindered biaryls with wedges on the ring bonds flanking the biaryl bond: draw one ring entirely with plain bonds, and the other with two solid wedges (one at the biaryl bond and one opposite) connected by an unwedged bold bond in even-membered rings (unless that bond is a ring fusion). A single wedge directly at the biaryl bond is acceptable; all other ring bonds remain plain, and wedges on distant substituents must never be used as the sole indication of the biaryl configuration.
- Use Fischer projections only for carbohydrates or where they are certain to be understood, and avoid them where ambiguity is possible; a 90° rotation gives the enantiomer, and horizontal Fischer projections of non-polymers are not acceptable.
- Use Haworth projections only when certain to be understood (carbohydrates and related compounds such as inositols), drawing the bottom ring bond bold when wedges are present; prefer flat Mills depictions in general.
- The H-dot, H-dash, and H-circle conventions are strongly deprecated.

## Stereochemistry: non-tetrahedral centers and metal complexes

- Draw every non-tetrahedral center so it is clearly recognizable and cannot be confused with another configuration; do not use the styles below for other configurations.
- Do not use polyhedral symbols that include lone pairs (such as TBPY-3 or TBPY-4).
- Never draw T-shaped, trigonal planar, or trigonal pyramidal centers with implicit ligands: draw all three bonds explicitly and label the center as a single atom.
- Draw T-shaped centers with three strictly horizontal or vertical plain bonds (by default, two vertical and one to the left; the other three orthogonal orientations are also preferred) and no wedges; carbon and nitrogen centers are never T-shaped; do not draw T-shaped centers of unknown configuration; describe them in the text instead.
- Draw trigonal planar centers with three plain bonds at equal angles; to emphasize planarity, use one plain bond, one solid wedge, and one hashed wedge about 60° apart, with the plain bond bisecting the opposite angle (place the solid wedge below the hashed wedge when horizontal).
- Draw trigonal pyramidal centers with one plain bond, one hashed wedge (>90° and <180° apart), and one solid wedge between them (>90° from the plain bond), or with two plain bonds and one wedge when no fourth ligand can be inferred; avoid one plain bond with two matching wedges, three-wedge forms, and planar-looking geometries.
- If all single-bonded neighbors of a trigonal pyramidal atom bearing a double bond are stereocenters, change one plain single bond to a wedge even though it joins two stereocenters; a wedged double bond is acceptable, not preferred.
- Draw square-planar centers symmetric about the vertical axis, with two solid wedges below (>90° apart) and two hashed wedges above; four plain bonds at 90° (with bisectors along the axes) are acceptable, and are preferred when all four ligands lie in the plane; avoid placing bonds along the axes.
- Draw four-coordinate square pyramids with two solid and two hashed wedges all pointing below the center, making the angle between the solid wedges smaller than that between the hashed wedges, and the solid wedges less than 150% as long as the hashed wedges; use plain four-bond forms only if achiral or of unknown configuration.
- Draw see-saw centers with two vertical plain bonds, a downward solid wedge, and an upward hashed wedge (bisected by the horizontal axis), or with two horizontal plain bonds and both wedges pointing down; plain-bond forms require collinear axial bonds.
- Draw trigonal bipyramids from the side with two vertical axial plain bonds, one horizontal plain bond, a downward solid wedge, and an opposing upward hashed wedge; a top view (three equatorial plain bonds with collinear solid and hashed axial wedges) is acceptable, but side views with matching upper or lower wedges are not acceptable.
- Draw five-coordinate square pyramids from the front with a vertical plain apical bond and two solid and two hashed wedges symmetric about the vertical axis: place the solid wedges below the center and the hashed wedges below them with the apex up (or the inverted form with the apex down) only when the central atom is not coplanar with the four equatorial ligands; place the solid wedges below and hashed wedges above (with the apex up or down) only when it is coplanar. From above, four equally spaced plain equatorial bonds plus one apical wedge are acceptable, not preferred.
- Draw octahedral centers symmetric about the vertical axis, with two vertical plain bonds, two downward solid wedges, and two upward hashed wedges; use plain-bond forms only if achiral or of unknown configuration.
- Draw trigonal prisms with two plain bonds on one side and two solid and two hashed wedges on the other; strongly avoid forms implying four ligands are coplanar with the center, as well as forms with excessive stereobonds.
- Use all-plain-bond forms for non-tetrahedral centers only when the center is achiral or its configuration is unknown; known chirality requires wedges and hashes.
- Do not use the four-coordinate square-pyramidal or see-saw styles for a carbon-group (or isoelectronic) center.

## Stereochemistry: perspective, double bonds, other configurations, mixtures

- Use perspective only for ring systems (usually bridged ones) unless illustrating a 3D concept; view the structure from above and to the right (nearer atoms lower), though a view from the left is acceptable, not preferred.
- Show the front-to-back order of crossing bonds with a gap in the rear bond (at least twice the bond width, or wider at low resolution); the depicted crossing order overrides the lower-is-nearer convention, but strongly avoid conflicts between the two.
- Interpret a perspective diagram as showing the absolute configuration at every stereocenter not marked with a wavy bond; use wavy bonds for unspecified centers, and use a flat depiction if the absolute configuration is unknown.
- Emphasize perspective only with solid wedges or bold bonds, never with hashed wedges or dashed/hashed lines; wedges must agree with the perspective, and solid wedges must not be used for individual stereocenters within a perspective ring system.
- Let an accurate polycyclic depiction take precedence over standard double-bond geometry (all four substituents may lie on one side).
- Apply the same rules to odd cumulenes.
- Contracted labels on double bonds are acceptable for unspecified configuration, but because their placement may imply a configuration, prefer explicit bonds.
- Draw planar chirality in perspective: orient the planar unit perpendicular to the page with solid wedges, or keep it in the plane with wedges on the attached bridge or substituents.
- Draw helicenes with a pair of solid wedges at one end (connected by an unwedged bold bond in even-membered rings) and optionally a pair of hashed wedges at the other end, with no wedges elsewhere.
- Draw Möbius strips using the front-to-back order of crossing bonds, optionally reinforced there by one solid and one hashed wedge consistent with the crossing, and no wedges elsewhere.
- Draw molecular propellers like hindered biaryls.
- Do not conflate known absolute, unknown absolute, racemic, enantioenriched, unknown, unspecified, and relative configurations.
- Indicate mixtures and relative configuration with explanatory text: draw stereoisomers in the same or mirrored orientations joined by "and" (never "+"), or draw one structure labeled "and enantiomer"; place the text nearby (preferably below or to the right) and never closer to another diagram.
- State enantiomer ratios only when both enantiomers are drawn, ordered left to right; label racemic mixtures explicitly, as an unlabeled pair does not imply a 50:50 mixture.
- Avoid using "racemate", "rac", "relative", and "rel" as structural labels.

## Reaction schemes and curved arrows

- Draw the opposing arrow of a single-electron transfer only if needed; it is redundant and sometimes omitted.
- Connect resonance forms with a double-headed arrow (↔), never with an equilibrium arrow.
- Use ⇄ for a reversible reaction and = for a stoichiometric relation as notation conventions.
- Arrange reactants so that electron pushing proceeds from left to right where possible.
